claim: To cut a notch/pocket into a curved surface (e.g. a cylinder's rim) so the cut's back wall follows the base object's own curvature instead of coming out flat/artificial: after the initial boolean cutter shape is placed, boolean-subtract a second shape (matched/aligned to the base object's own radius) FROM THE CUTTER OBJECT ITSELF before it cuts the base -- the base object's boolean result then inherits a correctly curved back wall automatically, without manually modeling or projecting a curved cutter from scratch.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-14, watched full video): at 2:30-2:46, a rectangular notch cutter's flat back wall is fixed by boolean-subtracting a radius-matched cylinder from the cutter object itself, so the cutter's own shape (and thus the resulting notch) inherits the correct curvature.
rejected_alternative: Manually modeling or projecting a curved cutter shape from scratch to match the base object's curvature
reason: Boolean-editing the cutter itself lets the boolean solver handle matching the curvature automatically, rather than manually shaping a cutter to match by eye.

claim: 'Stealing' surface geometry for a conformal panel line/recess on a compound-curved surface: select and duplicate (Shift+D) the existing face patch across the curved region, separate it into its own object (P > Selection), trim its edges as needed, inset it (I) to define a boundary, delete the resulting outer border ring, and use this patch as the boolean cutter cut back into the main body -- guarantees the recess exactly matches the underlying curvature since the cutter geometry came directly from that surface, rather than being drawn or modeled independently and risking misalignment.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 3:25-3:55, a face patch is duplicated and separated from an existing curved corner, trimmed/inset, and used as a boolean cutter for a panel line that then perfectly matches the original surface's curvature.
rejected_alternative: Drawing/modeling a custom cutter shape independently and hoping it aligns with the compound curve
reason: This is a second independent source (after RileyB3D's advanced-hardsurface build) converging on extracting boolean cutters directly from the host geometry itself to guarantee curvature matching on compound-curved surfaces.

claim: MeshMachine's 'Offset Cut' tool, run on a boolean-cut boundary edge on a curved surface, generates an equidistant buffer ring of quads pushed outward on both sides of the seam -- creating clearance so a subsequent standard edge bevel (Ctrl+B) doesn't collapse/overlap against nearby dense or unevenly-spaced vertices the way a direct bevel on the raw boolean seam would.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 5:08-5:48, a direct Ctrl+B bevel on a spherical body's boolean cutout boundary collapses into overlapping triangles; running MeshMachine's Offset Cut first generates a buffer ring of quads that gives a subsequent bevel clean clearance.
rejected_alternative: Beveling the raw boolean seam directly without first creating buffer clearance
reason: This is a second independent source (after Blender Bros' curvy/organic-shapes video) converging on MeshMachine's Offset Cut as the fix for bevel-collapse on dense curved boolean seams.

claim: When a boolean cut through a smooth-shaded curved surface (e.g. a cylinder through a sphere) produces long-range shading streaks/gradient pinching across the whole surface (caused by the boolean generating large n-gons spanning multiple poles), add loop cuts to increase the CUTTER object's own subdivision density before the boolean runs -- Blender transfers those extra cuts onto the boolean boundary wall, localizing the resulting n-gons into a narrow rim strip instead of letting them span the whole surface, eliminating the long-distance shading artifact without manual retopology.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 7:40-8:05, adding loop cuts to a boolean cutter cylinder localizes the resulting n-gons at the boundary into a narrow rim strip instead of letting shading-stretch artifacts span the entire sphere's surface, without retopologizing the sphere itself.
rejected_alternative: Manually retopologizing the sphere's surface after the boolean to fix the long-range shading streaks
reason: Increasing the cutter's own density before the boolean confines the resulting bad topology to a narrow strip at the cut boundary, avoiding the need to manually fix shading artifacts spread across the whole target surface afterward.

claim: To create a countersunk/flared chamfer around a boolean-cut hole (e.g. a screw hole, port, or o-ring groove) non-destructively: enter Edit Mode on the live cutter object, select the perimeter that will define the chamfer, flip its face normals (Alt+N), then apply a standard edge bevel (Ctrl+B) to that flipped selection -- the boolean solver interprets the beveled volume in reverse, producing a clean outward-flared chamfer on the resulting hole in the base object, while the cutter (and thus the whole setup) stays live and fully editable.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 9:32-10:05, flipping the normals on a boolean cutter cylinder's top perimeter before beveling it produces a countersunk, flared chamfer on the resulting hole in the base object, live and non-destructively.
rejected_alternative: Beveling the hole's rim directly on the base object after the boolean is applied (destructively)
reason: Beveling the cutter (with flipped normals) instead of the boolean's own resulting geometry keeps the whole setup non-destructive and re-editable, since the chamfer lives on the cutter rather than being baked into the base object.
